title: Economic Outlook and the Labor Market
summary: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a speech outlining his economic outlook, describing the economy as growing at roughly potential pace (~2% GDP in 2025) with similar or slightly faster growth expected for 2026. He characterized the labor market as roughly in balance, with unemployment at 4.3% in March following a stabilization after reaching 4.5% in November 2025. On inflation, PCE rose an estimated 2.8% year-over-year through February with core at 3.0%, and Jefferson stated he remains committed to returning inflation to the 2% target.
key_points: GDP expanded approximately 2% in 2025, slightly slower than 2024, with 2026 outlook similar or slightly faster
PCE inflation estimated at 2.8% and core PCE at 3.0% for the 12 months ending February 2026
Unemployment rate rose from 4.0% in January 2025 to 4.5% in November 2025, then stabilized at 4.3% in March 2026
March payrolls added 178,000 jobs; three-month average through Q1 2026 is approximately 70,000 jobs/month
Describes current labor market as 'low-hire, low-fire' state with firms cautious about expanding workforces
Tariffs and elevated energy prices pose upside risks to inflation forecast; strong productivity and deregulation may help disinflation
why_it_matters: This speech from a Federal Reserve Vice Chair provides insight into the FOMC's current thinking ahead of potential rate decisions. The speaker acknowledges progress stalling on inflation, maintains commitment to the 2% target, and sees roughly balanced risks to the dual mandate. Markets will monitor whether this cautious but committed stance aligns with pricing of the federal funds rate path.
macro_context: Jefferson describes a mixed macro picture: growth is proceeding near potential but with elevated uncertainty from geopolitical risks and energy prices. Inflation remains well above target with recent progress stalled by tariffs. The labor market has cooled from 2024 pace but stabilized at levels near estimated natural rate. The speaker sees risks to both sides of the Fed's dual mandate.
